tossups.text: People near this concept are said to "see with blinding sight" in one poem. This concept is called a "slave to fate, chance, kings, and desperate men" in a John Donne poem telling it to "be not proud". A poem by Dylan Thomas commands the listener to "rage, rage against" this concept, because "old age should burn and rave at close of day". For 10 points, what event happens to everyone at the end of their life?
acceptableAnswers: accept the dying of the light

tossups.text: Early in this work, a salesman arrives with a copy of the Arabian Nights for his cousin, the protagonist, and a new greyhound for his nephew, the protagonist's son. Another section describes a Madam's Yorkshire upbringing and the death of her brother in Canada, before the scene shifts to the boudoir of a Polish whore named Louise. In Chapter 9 a young woman with black teeth performs the song "Snow," which reminds the main character of the first time he "worshipped a woman," a feeling he no longer has for his own wife. The next chapter sees the protagonist accompany his father-in-law and O-hisa to see Morning Glory Diary, one of many puppet plays attended over the course of this novel. A letter from Takanatsu reveals that Hiroshi knows about his mother's infidelity with Aso and the coming dissolution of Misako and Kaname's marriage in, for 10 points, what work by Junichiro Tanizaki.

This man's body was burnt on a pyre by his freedman Philip. He was proclaimed a perfect commander because he had military knowledge, excellence, prestige, and luck in a speech by Cicero. One of his rivals quipped that "the enemy would have won if they had a commander who was a winner" instead of this man. Lucullus objected to losing his Asiatic command to this man. He worked with Quintus Caecilius Metellus Pius to put down the revolt of Sertorius. This victor at Dyrrachium was assigned Hispania at the Lucca conference. He was given extraordinary powers by the Lex Gabinia to hunt down Cilician pirates. Pothinus convinced Ptolemy XIII to betray this man in Egypt and send his head to a rival who had beaten him at the battle of Pharsalus. For 10 points, name this Roman who was part of the First Triumvirate along with Crassus and Julius Caesar.

Strains of this virus include MEF-1, Mahoney, and Saukett. This enterovirus binds to CD155, which is sometimes called its namesake receptor. Karl Landsteiner was the first to identify this virus, which causes a disease first discovered by Jakob Heine. The first vaccine against this virus used inactivated cultures, in contrast to the attenuated viruses used in the Sabin vaccine against it. Jonas Salk developed the first vaccine against this virus. For 10 points, name this virus, which causes a paralysis-inducing disease that affected Franklin Roosevelt.

An entry in this collection describes a "System" that "strangles talent" and "poisons the soul" and opens by describing a scene in which a mechanical monster abducts a child whose mother later muses "I just can‟t get that monster out of my mind." Another piece in this collection ends by dubbing the title man‟s life "a minor but perilous triumph of being over nothingness" after earlier describing that man fidgeting with a book of poems by Mao. This collection, which is divided into sections titled "Lifestyles in the Golden Land," "Personals", and "Seven Places of the Mind," contains "Comrade Laski, C.P.U.S.A. (M.-L.)," and appears after the "Introduction" in We Tell Ourselves Stories in Order to Live. A five-year old named Susan is fed acid and peyote by her mother in this collection‟s title essay, which describes the dissolution of San Francisco‟s Haight-Ashbury district. For 10 points, name this essay collection by Joan Didion that takes its title from Yeats‟ "The Second Coming."
acceptableAnswers: We Tell Ourselves Stories in Order to Live: Collected Nonfiction before mention

tossups.text: David McClelland developed a theory of this psychological concept mostly used in work-based managerial contexts. Henry Murray paired this concept with "press," or outside motivations, in his creation of 28 scored ratings for these in the Thematic Apperception Test. Clayton Altdorfer's Existence, Relatedness, and Growth, or ERG, model extends the most famous rubric for analyzing these, which has esteem as the penultimate level. Distinguished from wants by the negative effects of not fulfilling them are, For 10 points, what psychological motivations classified into a hierarchy by Abraham Maslow?

An author with this surname used the name Acton Bell to publishThe Tenant of Wildfell Hall. A novel byan author with this surname included Thrushcross Grange in a novel about Heathcliff and Catherine Earnshaw. An author with this surname wrote about Bertha Mason burning Thornfield Hall in a novel whose title character marries Rochester.Wuthering HeightsandJane Eyreare by authors with, for ten points, whatsurname shared by sisters Anne, Emily, and Charlotte?

Infection by Diphyllobothrium tapeworms can occasionally cause a deficiency of this molecule. Deficiency of this molecule is the most common cause of a subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord called Lichtheim's disease. A deficiency of this molecule causes elevated methylmalonyl-CoA ("methyl-malonyl-co-A") levels and can be diagnosed with the Schilling test. Approximately 90 percent of patients who have a disease caused by deficiency of this molecule have parietal cell autoantibodies present. Folate supplementation is prescribed to treat a deficiency of this molecule characterized by hypersegmented neutrophils. Defects in intrinsic factor production lead to deficiencies in the absorption of this molecule, causing pernicious anemia. For 10 points, name this cobalt-containing B vitamin.

A woman in a white dress is shown falling before a Madonna in this painter's Il Penseroso, and horseback riders approach a Gothic cathedral in his The Return. Another of his works portrays a palace made of clouds as an angel bids farewell, and this man depicted a thunderstorm transitioning to a calm river as seen from Mount Holyoke. In another series, hunters pursue deer across a rugged landscape in the 'Savage' section, while a colossal statue is shown beheaded in the 'Destruction' section. Depicted by Asher Durand alongside William Cullen Bryant in Kindred Spirits, For 10 points, name this American romantic painter of The Voyage of Life and The Course of Empire, the founder of the Hudson River School.

The behavior of ideal varieties of these substances can be described by the Thiele (THEEL) modulus. Those "perfect" varieties of these substances are limited only by the rate of diffusion. Metallic examples of these substances, such as Raney nickel, often function through adsorption. These substances can be classified as homogeneous or heterogeneous depending on their phase relative to their substrate. The action of these substances can be represented as a reduction in the height of the peak on a reaction energy profile diagram. Biological variants of these substances are called enzymes. For 10 points, name these substances that lower activation energy and increase reaction rate.

This category includes anyone who kills for a living, such as fishermen; anyone whose work involved contact with human bodily fluids; and anyone who ate or worked with dead cattle. Their rights were eventually protected in the Poona Pact. Falling below the Sudra on the varna scale, they were dubbed the Harijan, or "Children of God," by Gandhi. For 10 points, name these lowest members of a society that subscribes to the Hindu caste system.

On hearing that an actress is a "vision of eternal grace" and a "poem," a character created by this author remarks that he "thinks she's got her mouth open." That character investigates a murder at a house surrounded by "desolate marshes," the Muldoon Manor. A character created by this author teaches his student about the Library of Alexandria after enclosing a letter inside The Couch of Eros. That man is questioned about a "carnal embrace" before encouraging his student to solve Fermat's Last Theorem. This author of The Real Inspector Hound created the "hermit of Sidley Park'', Septimus Hodge. In one play by this author, a character watches the Tradegians perform The Murder of Gonzago after winning 92 coin flips in a row. For 10 points, name this playwright of Arcadia and Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are Dead.

Poseidon struck one of these creatures with his trident when it attempted to rape Amymone ("eh-meh-MOH-nay"). Another of these beings named Ampelos was gored and killed after mocking the goddess Selene, and his body was turned into a grape vine. After picking up an instrument that Athena had cursed, one of these beings subsequently died by being flayed alive. King Midas received the golden touch for sheltering one of these creatures, and he judged a competition between Apollo and one of these creatures named Marsyas. For 10 points, name these creatures in Greek mythology who attend to Dionysus and chase after wood nymphs.

This work enumerates twelve rights of a sovereign, and describes four causes of ignorance in a section titled "Of the Kingdom of Darkness." This work claims that there is no summum bonum, or universal good, but supports the establishment of a "Christian Commonwealth" to escape a "war of all against all," a state of nature that makes life "nasty, brutish, and short." For 10 points, name this work in which Thomas Hobbes defends the English monarchy, titled for a biblical monster.

This god partly names a NASA "Regolith Explorer" that took geological samples from the asteroid Bennu. Serapis is a Greco-Egyptian syncretization of this god with the Apis bull. This green-skinned god's body was recovered by his wife after he was dismembered into fourteen pieces by his brother Set. This god is often depicted in hieroglyphs holding a crook and flail. For ten points, name this Egyptian god of the dead, the husband of Isis.

His short poems include the Ruins of Rome and Visions of the World's Vanity, which are collected among his Complaints. He instructed the "sweet " to "run softly" until he ends his song in one of his major poems, while he concluded another poem by asking that it be "for short time an endless monument." He compared himself to the "culver on the bared bough" in the 89th and final sonnet of his sequence Amoretti, which is sometimes paired with his "Epithalamion." For 10 points, name this English poet better known for his epic featuring Britomart and the Red Cross Knight, The Fairie Queene.

This country's capital city hosted a 1986 summit between Mikhail Gorbachev and Ronald Reagan that eventually led to the Intermediate Nuclear Forces Treaty. In the year 1000, a chieftain named Thorgeir decided this country would practice Christianity though pagans would not be harassed. A period of internal clan violence in this country is called the Age of the Sturlungs, and involved this country's great writer of sagas, Snorri Sturluson. Gatherings at the Law Rock in this country led to the establishment of the world's oldest parliament, the Althing. For 10 points, what European island nation between Scandinavia and Greenland is governed from Reykjavik?

In a novel by an author with this surname, a eugenicist lectures his Singaporean secretary Naden about the coming "United States of Mankind" while on an Anthropological Mission in Malaya. An Auckland literary don with this surname was posthumously portrayed as the narcissistic philanderer "Karl" in his daughter Charlotte Grimshaw's memoir The Mirror Book. A novel by an author with this surname ends with a girl nicknamed "Little Womey" and "Looloo" fleeing Spa House in Annapolis after "Mothering" drinks a cyanide-laced cup of tea. Randall Jarrell's "An Unread Book" is an introduction to a novel by an author with this surname, in which the alcoholic Henny is tormented by the bizarre baby talk of her husband, the civil servant Sam Pollitt. For 10 points, the Australian author of The Man Who Loved Children had what surname and the first name Christina?

Alfred Hitchcock's Rope appears to use only one of this type of shot, but actually contains several of these with cuts in between. Similarly, cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki used several of these shots to make Birdman seem like it was shot in one take. It's not a tracking shot, but Park Chan-wook used this technique on a hallway fight scene in Oldboy for nearly three minutes. Until digital cameras came about, directors were often forced to use this technique so that the film didn't run out. Lubezki again used this type of take for a seventeen minute long establishing shot at the opening of Gravity. For ten points, name this camera technique in which a shot lasts uninterrupted for an above-normal duration.
acceptableAnswers: accept clear-knowledge equivalents until “For ten points

tossups.text: The Stentz algorithm is a dynamic variant of an earlier algorithm to accomplish this task in which the cost function can vary with time. This task can be carried out via a dynamic programming algorithm that operates on a series of states in a Markov model, called the Viterbi algorithm. Another algorithm for accomplishing this task relies on a heuristic function to estimate future costs; that algorithm, which takes the previous nodes visited into account and uses a priority queue to keep track of nodes yet to be visited, is called A-star. The frst single-source algorithm for doing this task was a greedy algorithm that always chooses the next node with the smallest tentative distance. For 10 points, identify this task accomplished by Dijkstra's algo-rithm, which consists of minimizing the distance between source and destination nodes on a graph.
acceptableAnswers: finding the most probable sequence of states

parts.text: Name this object which contains all points in space. Through this object, Daneri can see every point in the universe.
The short story "The Aleph" is by this Argentine writer, who wrote about the murder of Stephen Albert by Dr. Yu Tsun in "The Garden of Forking Paths."
In another of Borges's short stories, one of these institutions "of Babel" is home to an infinite number of 410-page books.

bonuses.leadin: The poet Carlos Daneri keeps this object in his basement, leading to him becoming enraged when a businessman threatens to tear his house down. For 10 points each--

parts.text: Name this poem which begins in the Malvern Hills, and in which William sees the titular agricultural worker.
Piers Plowman is attributed to this 14th-century Englishman, though only circumstantial evidence links him to the work.
The second part of Piers Plowman introduces this female character, whose marital misfortune is contrasted with the path of the Lady Holy Church.

bonuses.leadin: It ends with a search for three men named Do-Well, Do-Bet, and Do-Best. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this war in which von Moltke won the Battle of Sedan. This war was partly sparked by the editing of the Ems Dispatch.

France's loss to Prussia sparked this movement aimed at regaining land lost during the war, such as Alsace ("ahl-sahss") and Lorraine. Georges Boulanger ("zhorzh boo-lawn-zhay") was nicknamed this movement's "Général ("zheh-neh-rahl")" for his inveterate support of it.

This historian downplayed the impact of the Franco-Prussian War and revanchisme on French society in his book Peasants into Frenchmen, which argues that rural inhabitants were largely ambivalent to the war. This historian gave the public television lecture series The Western Tradition.

bonuses.leadin: Helmuth von Moltke the Elder wrote a firsthand account of this war that Archibald Forbes translated. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Identify this relationship which is exhibited by a cube and an octahedron.
An octahedron and a cube are examples of these regular solids named after an ancient Greek philosopher.

One can generate new polyhedra in this process in which the faces of a polyhedron are extended in the plane. This process cannot be applied to a cube or a tetrahedron, while doing it to an icosahedron generates 59 distinct polyhedra.

bonuses.leadin: These structures are formed by reciprocation, in which a one-to-one correspondence is established between faces and vertices of a polyhedron and this structure. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this genre, which was typically used for love poetry by Tibullus. This genre consists of alternating lines of six and five metrical feet, which form this genre's namesake couplets.
This Roman poet's Amores (am-OR-ayz) imagines Cupid stealing a metrical foot to force him to write elegiac couplets. This poet also wrote the Metamorphoses.

This Roman poet wrote six elegies addressed to her lover Cerinthus. This female poet's works were published among Tibullus's poems, encouraging some modern scholars to speculate about their authorship.

bonuses.leadin: Catullus used this genre for his two-line eighty-fifth poem, which begins "I hate and I love." For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this man who used the subtitle "The Fierce People" in a book about the Yanomami.
Yanomami indigenous people live along the Amazon River, where Chagnon studied them mostly on the tributary Maravaca in this country, also home to Angel Falls.
Patrick Tierney accused Chagnon of starting a measles epidemic that killed 20% of the Yanomami in a book entitled Darkness in this legendary city of treasure.

bonuses.leadin: This anthropologist studied the chest-pounding duels used to settle grievances among a group of indigenous people whose word for menstruation translates literally as "squatting." For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this 1894 collection of short stories, most of which are about animals. It is the best known work of the British-Indian author Rudyard Kipling.
This character in The Jungle Book first appears in Kipling's story "In the Rukh." This "man-cub" is raised by a pack of wolves who protect him from the tiger Shere Khan ["share" kahn].
This character from The Jungle Book protects a human family from the cobras Nag and Nagaina after being saved from drowning. This mongoose's name comes from the sound that he makes.

bonuses.leadin: One story in this work is about a white seal named Kotick who finds a better home after he sees many other seals being killed in the Bering Sea. For ten points each:

parts.text: To take up water under high salinity, mangrove tissues often reduce this energetic quantity by accumulating ions. At and beyond the turgor loss point, this quantity is usually equal to the total water potential.
Mangrove roots deposit suberin in the radial and transverse cell walls of endodermal cells to form this structure, which acts as a diffusion barrier to prevent salt from entering the apoplast.

Some mangrove plants simply trap salt by using sodium-proton pumps to concentrate it into these storage organelles. A "central" one of these organelles in plant cells stores water and maintains turgor pressure.

bonuses.leadin: Answer the following about halotolerance mechanisms evolved by mangrove plants, for 10 points each.

parts.text: Name this political figure assassinated in 1948. Another iconic photograph of this figure shows him reading on the floor next to a spinning wheel.

This photographer took the aforementioned photo of Gandhi next to a spinning wheel. She was the first female American war photojournalist, and her photograph of the Fort Peck Dam appeared on the first cover of Life.

A 1934 photo shows Bourke-White positioning her camera atop one of these locations. Charles C. Ebbets showed several workers eating lunch on a steel beam above Manhattan while constructing one of these locations.

bonuses.leadin: Henri Cartier-Bresson took the last photos of this political figure and also photographed his funeral. For 10 points each:

parts.text: On a sphere, this shape is analogous to a straight line and has the same diameter and center as the sphere. These shapes perfectly divide the sphere into two hemispheres.
Since all lines on spheres are great circles, they do not remain equidistant and will always intersect at opposite points and, therefore, cannot have this property.

Since lines on a sphere cannot be parallel, they violate this mathematician's fifth postulate, meaning many aspects of spherical geometry contradict this "father of geometry's" namesake mathematical system.

bonuses.leadin: For 10 points each, answer these questions about straight lines on a sphere:

parts.text: This brother of James the Greater wrote the Book of Revelation in addition to his Gospel and his Epistles.
Often identified as Levi, this author of the first synoptic Gospel was a tax collector before joining Jesus.
He had his own testimonial acts and was crucified on an X-shaped cross that now bears his name.

bonuses.leadin: Identify these members of the Twelve Apostles for 10 points each.

parts.text: Name this type of work exemplified by Gassire's Lute. In one of these works, Sogolon raises the title character, who defeats Sumanguru with an arrow.
This legendary king, who establishes Niani, titles a West African epic about the birth of the Mali empire.

In the Congolese Epic of Mwindo, the title character is sealed inside one of these objects, which is thrown into the river. The much later poem "Elegy For Alto" opens with a parenthetical noting the presence of these objects.

bonuses.leadin: Leo Frobenius collected a work of this type about a prince of Wagadu who fails to make noise while playing the harp, learning it will only make music if he goes into battle. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this hero who launched the Calydonian boar hunt and fell for Atalanta.
The Calydonian boar was sent by this goddess of virginity and the hunt after King Oeneus forgot to make a sacrifice to her. Atalanta was a favorite of this goddess, Apollo's twin sister.
Meleager's sister was Deianira, who's best-known for killing Heracles with a shirt stained with the blood of this centaur.

bonuses.leadin: This man's mother managed to save a strand of wood at his birth so that he couldn't die unless it was burnt, but she got angry at him and burned it up. For 10 points each:

parts.text: This Chinese practice, named from the words for "wind-water", is used to harmonize buildings with their surroundings using qi (chee).

In Chinese astrology, this cycle of animals is supposed to determine one's personality, as primarily assigned by year. Its Western counterpart assigns people to one of twelve constellations representing parts of the year.
This is the only fictitious animal in the zodiac. Chinese examples of these animals do not typically have wings, unlike Western examples.

bonuses.leadin: Answer some questions about Chinese traditional astrology, for 10 points each:

parts.text: Name these figures, which include Brunhilde, who is saved by Siegfried.
Valkyries carry dead men to this location. This massive hall in Asgard is where men feast until called during Ragnarök.
The other half of dead soldiers will go to Fólkvangr, a hall belonging to this goddess. This goddess of beauty and fertility rides a chariot pulled by cats.

bonuses.leadin: These figures serve mead from the udder of the goat Heiðrún ["high-druhn"], while men feast on the great boar Særímnir ["saer-im-neer"]. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this play in which Pozzo and Lucky show up while Estragon and Vladimir are doing the title action.
This absurdist author who wrote in French despite being from Ireland wrote Waiting for Godot.
This other Beckett drama, titled for a phase of a chess match, features one character unable to stand, another unable to sit, and two characters with no legs.

bonuses.leadin: (Extra) One character in this play gives a teary-eyed description of maps of the Holy Land. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this son of John I of Portugal who gathered a court at his house of Sagres. He's best known for sponsoring numerous naval expeditions down the coast of Africa.

Henry the Navigator's sponsorships paved the way for explorers like this man, who built on the success of Bartolomeu Dias by voyaging beyond the Cape of Good Hope in 1497. His trip is commemorated in The Lusiads.

Vasco da Gama arrived in India at this port city, also known as the "City of Spices." This city ruled by people called Zamorin attacked members of Pedro Cabral's expedition and were bombarded in retaliation.

bonuses.leadin: This man convinced his father to conquer the Moroccan city of Ceuta. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this George Bernard Shaw play in which Henry Higgins takes a bet to transform the cockney Eliza Doolittle into a lady.
This other Shaw character eventually gains the admiration of her daughter Vivie despite her work in the prostitution industry.
Shaw popularized this other playwright by publishing an extended essay on his "quintessence." His own plays include The League of Youth and Love's Comedy.

bonuses.leadin: In this play, Clara Hill becomes less snobbish and more critical after reading H. G. Wells. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Give this title of a late 1660s painting in the Rijksmuseum ("reeks-museum") by the same artist in which a man in gold rests his hands on a woman in red, whose religious affiliation has been debated.
acceptableAnswers: prompt on Portrait of a Couple as Isaac and Rebecca
Isaak en Rebekka by asking "what other title is given to the painting?"

parts.text: This Dutch painter of The Jewish Bride and The Night Watch depicted himself leaning out over a ledge in one of his dozens of self-portraits.

Rembrandt depicted his wife Saskia holding out a flower to the viewer in a painting of her as Flora, a goddess who stares at the viewer in this other painting. A blue spirit lunges out of a tree in this painting, which depicts the Three Graces dancing in an orange grove.

bonuses.leadin: This is the alternate title of a painting in which a girl in a red dress and a black hat rests her hands on a black picture frame. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name these rock structures whose upper surface defines the water table. Ogallala, Nebraska, is the namesake of a large example of these underground structures.
Aquifers often form in this type of fold, defined as having their youngest layers closest to the center of the fold.
London sits on a syncline aquifer made of this porous rock. The deposition of this rock from the Late Cretaceous forms a large cliff structure on the coast of Kent.

bonuses.leadin: These structures can be unconfined when connected to the surface by a permeable layer. For 10 points each:
